title: 22. Interview: Auto Scaling
summary: Interview Q&A for Auto Scaling — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Auto Scaling interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling, and when do you choose each?
**Answer:** Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances of the same size — 10 EC2s become 50. Vertical scaling (scaling up) makes each instance bigger — m5.large becomes m5.2xlarge. Horizontal is preferred for stateless workloads because it has no upper bound (you can keep adding instances), it does not cause downtime (new nodes join the pool while old ones serve), and it improves redundancy by spreading load across more failure domains. Vertical scaling is the right answer when an application cannot be horizontally partitioned — a single MySQL primary that needs more memory for a larger buffer pool, a JVM that needs more heap for in-memory analytics, or a stateful service like Redis where sharding adds complexity. Vertical scaling has an upper bound (the largest instance the cloud offers) and requires a restart when resizing, which means a brief outage. The mature pattern is horizontal for stateless frontends and vertical for stateful primaries, with sharding as the escape hatch when a stateful primary hits the vertical ceiling.
**Visual:**
```
horizontal:  [n1][n2][n3] -> [n1][n2][n3][n4][n5][n6]   (+ instances)
vertical:    [m5.large]    -> [m5.2xlarge]               (bigger instance, restart)
stateless  -> horizontal (no upper bound, no downtime)
stateful   -> vertical (simpler) or shard (when vertical maxed)
```

### Q2. How does target tracking differ from step scaling?
**Answer:** Target tracking lets you specify a desired value for a metric — "keep average CPU at 50%" — and the platform computes the capacity adjustment needed to hold that target. If CPU is 80% with 10 instances, the platform reasons that 10 × (80/50) = 16 instances are needed and scales out to 16. It handles both scale-out and scale-in symmetrically, requires only one parameter (the target), and naturally smooths out fluctuations. Step scaling requires you to specify threshold bands and adjustment sizes — "+1 instance if CPU is 70–80%, +3 if 80–90%, +5 if above 90%" — which gives finer control but requires more tuning and asymmetry (you must specify separate scale-in and scale-out policies). Step scaling is preferred when you want non-linear response (a small breach adds a little, a large breach adds a lot) or when the metric does not scale linearly with capacity. Target tracking is the default for most modern workloads because it is simpler and self-balancing. Both can be combined: target tracking for normal operation, step scaling for emergency spikes.
**Visual:**
```
target tracking:  desired = current * (metric / target)
                  CPU 80%, target 50%, current 10 -> desired 16
step scaling:     breach bands -> fixed adjustments
                  CPU 70-80%: +1   80-90%: +3   >90%: +5
                  (requires separate scale-in policy)
```

### Q3. What is predictive scaling and when is it useful?
**Answer:** Predictive scaling uses machine learning models trained on historical traffic patterns (typically 14 days of CloudWatch data) to forecast demand and pre-scale the fleet before the demand arrives. It is useful for workloads with predictable diurnal or weekly patterns — a retail site that peaks at 10am and 8pm every day, a gaming service that spikes on weekend evenings, a tax-prep site that surges every April. AWS launched predictive scaling for EC2 ASGs in 2022; it composes with target tracking (predictive pre-warms, target tracking fine-tunes in real time). The benefit is that you avoid the latency of reactive scaling — by the time CPU crosses 70% and a new instance boots (60–180s), users have already felt slowness; predictive scaling has the capacity ready before the spike. The trade-off is that it only works for predictable patterns; a viral news event or an unplanned product launch will not match the forecast, so reactive scaling is still required as a backstop. Amazon Prime Day uses predictive scaling to pre-warm ahead of the event.
**Visual:**
```
historical:  M T W T F S S  (14 days)
forecast:    tomorrow 9am spike -> pre-scale at 8:30am
reactive:    CPU > 70% at 9:05am -> scale out (too late, users felt it)
predictive:  capacity ready at 8:30 -> 0 latency at 9am spike
compose:     predictive pre-warm + target tracking fine-tune
```

### Q4. What is the role of cooldowns and warmup in auto scaling?
**Answer:** Cooldown is the quiet period after a scaling action during which the ASG will not perform another scale-in (and sometimes scale-out). Without cooldown, the system flaps: a brief CPU spike triggers scale-out, the new instances cause CPU to drop, scale-in triggers, the next spike finds the system under-provisioned, and the cycle repeats. A typical cooldown is 300 seconds, long enough for the system to stabilize at the new capacity. Warmup is the time a newly added instance takes to start serving traffic — boot the OS, start the application, pass health checks, register with the load balancer. During warmup, the instance's metrics should not be aggregated into the ASG's average because they do not reflect its eventual load; otherwise the policy sees a falsely low average and scales in prematurely. AWS lets you configure warmup per ASG (default 300s, often set to 60–120s for fast-booting stateless services, 600s for stateful). The trade-off is responsiveness versus stability: shorter values react faster but flap; longer values are stable but lag.
**Visual:**
```
scale-out at t=0  -> new instance warming (warmup=120s)
                  -> during warmup, metric excludes new instance
                  -> cooldown=300s blocks next scale-in until t=300
without cooldown: flap (out -> in -> out -> in) on noisy metrics
```

### Q5. How does Kubernetes HPA differ from the Cluster Autoscaler, and how do they compose?
**Answer:** HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales the number of Pod replicas within the existing node fleet. It watches a metric (CPU, memory, or custom via Prometheus adapter) every 15–30 seconds and adjusts the Deployment's replica count. Pod startup is in milliseconds, so HPA responds in seconds — but only if there is node capacity to schedule the new Pods. The Cluster Autoscaler (CA) is a separate controller that watches for Pending Pods (Pods the scheduler cannot place because no node has capacity) and provisions new nodes via the cloud API. Node provisioning takes 60–180 seconds, so CA is much slower than HPA. They compose as a two-tier system: HPA absorbs short spikes by packing more Pods onto existing nodes (which can be over-committed for a brief period); CA handles sustained growth by adding nodes when Pods stay Pending. The trade-off is that the two tiers must be tuned together — if HPA scales too aggressively, you trigger CA unnecessarily; if CA cooldowns are too long, Pending Pods accumulate.
**Visual:**
```
spike -> HPA: replicas 5 -> 30 (within seconds, Pods in ms)
              if existing nodes have spare CPU/mem, Pods run
              else Pods go Pending
       -> CA: sees Pending -> provisions nodes (60-180s)
              new nodes register -> Pending Pods scheduled
two-tier: HPA = fast reactive within capacity; CA = slow node-level
```

### Q6. Why is scale-in harder than scale-out?
**Answer:** Scale-out is forgiving — adding capacity when load is high rarely causes problems beyond cost. Scale-in is dangerous because removing capacity can disrupt in-flight work, break quorum on stateful services, trigger cascading failures if too much is removed at once, or remove the wrong instance (e.g., one holding a database primary). Scale-in also has to choose *which* instance to terminate, and a bad choice can disrupt a tenant, a session, or a cache. The defensive patterns: terminate oldest-first (so newer instances with newer code stay); use termination protection on stateful nodes; drain from the load balancer before terminating (wait for in-flight requests to finish); respect PodDisruptionBudgets in Kubernetes (do not evict a Pod if it would drop a Deployment below its quorum); use smaller step sizes for scale-in than scale-out; use longer cooldowns for scale-in; and cap the rate of scale-in (e.g., no more than 10% of fleet per 5 minutes). Netflix's Chaos Monkey deliberately forces scale-in by terminating instances during business hours to expose weaknesses in termination handling.
**Visual:**
```
scale-out:  add capacity -> harmless (just costs money)
scale-in:   pick instance -> drain -> terminate
            risks: in-flight requests lost, quorum broken,
                   cache wiped, wrong instance picked, cascade
defenses:   oldest-first, drain before kill, PDBs, smaller steps,
            longer cooldowns, rate caps, Chaos Monkey to test
```

### Q7. How does spot instance integration change auto scaling economics?
**Answer:** Spot instances are spare cloud capacity offered at up to 90% discount, with the caveat that the cloud can reclaim them with 2 minutes' notice. Integrating spot into an ASG dramatically lowers cost for stateless, interruptible workloads. The pattern is a mixed-instance ASG: a baseline of on-demand instances (e.g., 30% of capacity) for stability and a spot tier (70%) for the bulk. Spot interruptions are handled by an interruption handler (AWS EventBridge → Lambda) that drains the instance and the ASG replaces it from the spot pool or, if the spot market is dry, falls back to on-demand. The cost savings are large — a fleet that is 70% spot costs roughly 30–40% of an all-on-demand fleet at the same capacity. The trade-off is operational complexity (interruption handling, capacity rebalancing, instance diversification across multiple instance types and AZs to ensure the spot pool can be satisfied) and the risk that a spot market drought during a peak forces on-demand fallback at higher cost. Amazon Prime Day uses spot for the burst tier with on-demand baseline.
**Visual:**
```
ASG mixed:  30% on-demand (baseline, always available)
            70% spot (cheap, can be reclaimed with 2 min notice)
interruption:  EventBridge -> Lambda drains -> ASG replaces
               if spot pool dry -> fall back to on-demand
cost:  ~30-40% of all-on-demand at same capacity
risk:  spot drought at peak -> forced on-demand at higher $/hr
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your ASG scales out but never scales in, leaving instances idle. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** First, verify the metric the scale-in policy watches. A common mistake is to scale out on CPU but scale in on a different metric (or not configure scale-in at all). With target tracking, scale-in is automatic — if it is not happening, the metric may be artificially elevated. Check for zombie processes or background daemons consuming CPU on idle instances, or a noisy neighbor (e.g., a log shipper) keeping CPU above the scale-in threshold. Second, check the cooldown — if it is set very long, scale-in waits too long. Third, check the warmup — if warmup is set longer than the actual boot time, newly added instances are excluded from the metric average for too long, making the policy think the fleet is more utilized than it is. Fourth, check termination policies — if the policy is "NewestInstance" with a min-size constraint, the ASG may not be able to terminate. Fifth, check for instance protection — if all instances have scale-in protection enabled, the ASG cannot terminate. Finally, check the desired capacity: someone may have manually set desired to a high value, overriding the policy.
**Visual:**
```
never scales in? check:
  1. scale-in policy configured (target tracking auto-scales in)
  2. cooldown too long? warmup too long?
  3. metric artificially elevated (zombie, log shipper, noisy neighbor)
  4. termination policy or instance protection blocking
  5. desired manually overridden
```

### Q2. Your service has a p99 latency spike every time the ASG scales out. What is happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The likely cause is that newly added instances are being added to the load balancer's target group before they are fully ready to serve traffic. The ASG launches an instance, it passes the ELB health check (often just a TCP check or a fast 200), and the ELB starts sending traffic — but the application is still warming up: JIT-compiling code, populating caches, establishing DB connection pools. Real requests hit a cold instance and take much longer than normal, spiking p99. The fix is to make the health check stricter — use an application-level endpoint (e.g., `/health/ready`) that returns 200 only after the app has warmed, and set the health check grace period long enough for the app to fully initialize. AWS calls this the "ELB health check grace period" on the ASG. Additionally, configure connection draining (deregistration delay) so that when an instance is being terminated, in-flight requests finish before the ELB stops sending new ones. For Kubernetes, use readiness probes (not just liveness probes) so that the service mesh and kube-proxy do not route to a Pod that is not ready.
**Visual:**
```
ASG launches -> ELB health check passes (TCP OK) -> traffic routed
              -> but app still warming (JIT, cache, DB pool)
              -> real requests slow -> p99 spikes
fix: stricter /health/ready check, longer grace period,
     connection draining on terminate, K8s readiness probes
```

### Q3. You are preparing for a product launch expecting 10× normal traffic. How do you architect auto scaling?
**Answer:** Do not rely on reactive scaling alone — a 10× spike will overwhelm any reactive system before it scales. Use a layered approach. First, use predictive scaling (or scheduled scaling) to pre-warm the fleet to the expected launch capacity 30 minutes before the event. For AWS, scheduled actions on the ASG set desired capacity to the predicted value at a specific time. Second, configure target tracking with a lower-than-normal target (e.g., 40% CPU instead of 70%) so the system scales out aggressively on the first sign of load. Third, ensure the max-size of the ASG is high enough — pre-request a quota increase if needed. Fourth, use multiple AZs for redundancy and to spread the load. Fifth, pre-warm dependent systems: databases (raise provisioned throughput on DynamoDB, scale up RDS), caches (populate), and CDNs (cache warm). Sixth, set up CloudWatch alarms on key metrics (throttles, 5xx, latency) with SNS notifications. Seventh, have a manual override plan — a runbook to set desired capacity directly if automation fails. Eighth, conduct a load test in staging a week before to validate the scaling. Amazon Prime Day and AWS re:Invent keynotes are operated this way.
**Visual:**
```
T-30min:  scheduled action -> desired 10x baseline (pre-warm)
launch:   target tracking at 40% CPU (aggressive scale-out)
          max-size raised, quota pre-approved
deps:     DynamoDB provisioned capacity pre-raised, CDN cache warmed
alarms:   throttles, 5xx, latency -> SNS -> oncall
fallback: runbook to set desired manually if automation fails
```

### Q4. Your team runs a Kafka consumer on Lambda with parallelization. How do you prevent a runaway consumer from scaling infinitely?
**Answer:** Lambda-Kinesis and Lambda-Kafka integrations scale based on shard or partition count, with a parallelization factor up to 10 batches per shard. Runaway scaling happens when the consumer cannot keep up with the producer and the platform keeps adding concurrent invocations, eventually hitting the account concurrency limit and starving other functions. Defenses: set a reserved concurrency on the consumer function (e.g., 200) so it cannot consume the entire account; use the `BisectBatchOnFunctionError` and `MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds` to drop poison pills rather than retrying forever; configure `OnFailure` to send failed batches to a DLQ/SQS; monitor `IteratorAge` — if it is climbing, the consumer is not keeping up and you need to add shards or optimize the function; raise the function's memory (and thus CPU) so it processes batches faster; offload heavy work to a downstream queue (SQS) and let Lambda fan out further. For Kafka specifically, ensure partitions are balanced — a hot partition causes uneven scaling. If the producer genuinely exceeds consumer capacity, the right answer is to scale the source (more shards/partitions) or move processing off Lambda to Fargate/EKS with more controlled scaling.
**Visual:**
```
Lambda-Kafka runaway:  parallelization factor x10, account concurrency 1000
defenses:
  - reserved concurrency on consumer (e.g., 200)
  - BisectBatchOnFunctionError, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds
  - OnFailure -> DLQ
  - monitor IteratorAge -> if climbing, add shards or optimize
  - raise memory (CPU scales with memory)
  - move heavy processing to Fargate if sustained > Lambda capacity
```

### Q5. You have a mix of long-lived WebSocket connections and HTTP requests on the same ASG. Auto scaling misbehaves. What do you do?
**Answer:** The fundamental problem is that the ASG's metric (typically CPU) does not capture the WebSocket load. A single instance can hold 10,000 open WebSockets at near-zero CPU and look underutilized to the autoscaler, which then scales in and drops 10,000 connections. The fix is to separate the two workloads. Run WebSockets on a dedicated ASG scaled by connection count (a custom metric pushed to CloudWatch) or on a service designed for long-lived connections (AWS API Gateway WebSocket, AWS AppSync, or a stateful service like Amazon ECS with service connect). Run HTTP requests on a separate ASG scaled by CPU or RPS. If you cannot separate, use a custom metric for the combined ASG that weights both CPU and connection count, e.g., `(cpu + connection_count / max_connections) / 2`. Configure the scale-in to use connection-aware termination: when terminating, drain WebSockets gracefully (send close frames, wait for clients to reconnect to other instances) and use a longer deregistration delay. For stateful workloads like this, consider sticky sessions at the load balancer and ensure the application can handle connection migration.
**Visual:**
```
mixed ASG (CPU + WebSockets) -> CPU looks low -> scale-in -> 10k WS dropped
fix:
  1. split: WS on dedicated ASG (scaled by conn count) + HTTP on another
  2. or use API Gateway WebSocket / AppSync / stateful ECS service
  3. custom metric: weighted (cpu + conn/max_conn) / 2
  4. graceful WS drain: close frames, longer deregistration delay
```

### Q6. Your Kubernetes HPA scales replicas but Pods go Pending and never schedule. What do you do?
**Answer:** Pods go Pending when the scheduler cannot find a node with enough allocatable CPU, memory, GPU, or other requested resources. First, run `kubectl describe pod <pending-pod>` and read the Events — the message tells you why (e.g., `0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient cpu`). Second, check the Pod's resource requests — if the developer set `requests: cpu: 4` on a node pool of 2-vCPU nodes, it will never fit; either lower the request or move to a larger instance pool. Third, check the Cluster Autoscaler — if it is enabled, it should provision a new node when it sees Pending Pods; if it does not, check CA logs, the node group's `maxSize`, IAM permissions, and whether the Pod has a `nodeSelector` that matches an existing pool. Fourth, check for taints and tolerations — a tainted node pool that the Pod does not tolerate is invisible to the scheduler. Fifth, check for Pod affinity/anti-affinity rules that may be too strict. Sixth, check whether existing nodes are underutilized but fragmented — a 4-vCPU node with 3 vCPU requested cannot fit a 2-vCPU Pod; the VPA recommendation mode or Descheduler can help compact Pods. Seventh, watch for resource quota limits at the namespace level.
**Visual:**
```
kubectl describe pod -> Events:
  0/12 nodes available: 12 Insufficient cpu
fix:
  - lower Pod requests OR move to larger instance pool
  - check CA: maxSize? IAM? nodeSelector match?
  - check taints/tolerations, affinity rules
  - compact underutilized nodes (Descheduler, VPA recommendations)
  - check namespace ResourceQuota
```

### Q7. A misconfigured scale-in removed 30% of your fleet during a peak, causing a cascade. How do you prevent recurrence?
**Answer:** A cascade like this typically happens because the scale-in policy removed too much too fast — for example, a step policy with "-10 instances if CPU < 30%" that fires during a brief lull inside a peak. The defensive layers: first, cap scale-in rate — most ASGs let you set `MaxInstanceLifetime` or use a custom Lambda to gate terminations to no more than X% per Y minutes. Second, use a longer cooldown for scale-in than scale-out (e.g., 600s scale-in vs 60s scale-out). Third, use target tracking instead of step scaling for scale-in — it scales in proportionally to the metric, not in fixed steps. Fourth, set a higher scale-in threshold band so brief lulls do not trigger removal (e.g., scale in only if CPU < 30% for 10 minutes, not 1 minute). Fifth, enable instance protection on a baseline fraction of the fleet (e.g., the first N instances) so the ASG can never go below a safety floor. Sixth, set up CloudWatch alarms on capacity and latency with SNS to alert oncall before the cascade. Seventh, post-incident, run Chaos Monkey or Fault Injection Simulator to validate termination behavior. Amazon and Netflix both use capacity floors and rate-limited scale-in to prevent exactly this failure mode.
**Visual:**
```
cascade:  step policy "-10 if CPU<30%" fires during brief lull -> 30% gone
prevention:
  - cap scale-in rate (max 10% per 5 min)
  - longer cooldown for scale-in (600s vs 60s scale-out)
  - target tracking for scale-in (proportional, not fixed step)
  - threshold band with sustained breach (CPU<30% for 10 min)
  - capacity floor: first N instances protected
  - CloudWatch alarm on capacity/latency -> SNS
  - validate with FIS / Chaos Monkey
```
